competencies.justification: Both demands of C-6.1 are verified independently against the transformation inventory. Demand one — explaining key natural phenomena — is the chapter's organising spine: 'The Complexity of Mapping the Earth' explains the oblate spheroid and projection distortion; 'The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans' explains the ocean's role in regulating climate through heat absorption, moisture and rainfall; 'Ocean currents' explains warm and cold currents and traces the Gulf Stream's causal effect on Western European coastal climate; 'Ocean trenches' explains an extreme physical environment; and every continent section explains a formation process — the Tibetan Plateau by Indo-Australian and Eurasian plate collision, the Urals by tectonic forces, volcanic activity and erosion, the European Plain by sediment deposition, the Colorado Plateau by sedimentary uplift and erosion. Demand two — how these phenomena are spatially distributed — is satisfied by the chapter's own architecture: 'The Continents: Variety on Land' announces a continent-by-continent tour and Asia, Europe, Africa, South America, North America and The Australian Continent each locate their landforms on a physical map. The concluding 'Before we move on …' synthesis names tectonic movements, erosion and deposition as the shaping processes, confirming the chapter's fundamental purpose. Complete removal of this competency would leave no chapter.

'The Complexity of Mapping the Earth' is a dedicated, architecturally distinct named section that could stand alone as a learning unit, satisfying Rule 5(a). Its entire subject is the representation and analysis of geographical data in map form: it establishes why every projection distorts, then requires the student to compare the Mercator and Robinson projections and evaluate the specific trade-off each makes, concluding that a fair understanding demands reading multiple projections rather than one. The section's own activity requires students to decode the colour language of physical maps, and that decoding is then applied throughout — 'Smaller water bodies and waterways' presents a classification table of seas, gulfs, bays, straits and canals to be read against named examples, the Asia section directs students back to the colour key to identify features on Fig. 1.11, the Europe section requires students to read the European Plain's extent against the political map and list the countries it covers, the Africa section requires them to trace the Nile's course, origin and direction of flow, the Australia section requires conclusions about landforms drawn from map colour alone, and the Tibetan Plateau section sets two satellite images from 1987 and 2021 against each other for difference-detection. This is analysis of data given in tables, diagrams and maps, not incidental illustration.

This C-code carries two distinct demands and each was verified independently. The demand for Indian perspectives on conservation is NOT met — the chapter states at 'The Continents: Variety on Land' that India's landforms were covered in Part 1 and deliberately restricts itself to other parts of the world, leaving only the opening reference to Bhudevi and Vasudha, which is not a conservation perspective. This caps the weight below Central. The second demand — advocating conservation and sustainability in the context of global climate change — is developed substantively and deliberately across multiple named sections, satisfying Rule 5(b), and the chapter's own organising logic makes that continuity explicit by framing the whole text with the Big Question 'How do human actions trigger environmental issues?'. 'The Great Barrier Reef' is a named section that closes on threats from overfishing, pollution and climate change and states that conservation is crucial, with coral bleaching attributed to human action; the oceans section requires students to reason about the consequence of plankton loss for oxygen; the Urals passage explains permafrost melt releasing stored greenhouse gases; the Steppes are explained as a global carbon sink; the Tibetan Plateau section evidences climate-driven snow-melt; the savannah, the Amazon, the Andes as a conservation hotspot, the Atacama fast-fashion emergency and Great Lakes contamination each name human-caused degradation; and 'Before we move on …' synthesises desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change into an argument for managing these features wisely for sustainable development.

Rule 5(b) is satisfied: the correlation of livelihood patterns with landforms, resource availability and climatic conditions is developed deliberately across many named sections, and the chapter's own organising logic makes the continuity evident because 'The Continents: Variety on Land' announces that the tour will examine each landform for 'in what ways they are connected to life'. The Gobi Desert section correlates harsh climate and sparse vegetation with seasonal herd migration to pastures fed by underground water; the Steppes section presents the yurt of the nomad; the European Plain section correlates fertile soil with wheat, barley, rye and potato cultivation, rivers with trade and transport, and flat terrain and favourable climate with the growth of Moscow, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Warsaw; the Africa section correlates the Sahara with nomadic herding of sheep, goats and camels, oasis settlement, underground dwellings that stay cool in summer and warm in winter, and ancient gold and salt trade routes, then correlates the Nile's irrigation with wheat, barley, flax, fruit and vegetable cultivation, fishing, hydroelectric power and transport; the Rockies section correlates the range with mining, hydropower, tourism and agriculture and with indigenous communities that depended on its rivers, forests and wildlife; the Appalachians with coal, timber and gas industries; the Great Lakes with shipping and municipal water supply; and the Australian Continent with the Spinifex people's 25,000-year desert residence and present-day tourism. The competency is not, however, the chapter's fundamental organising purpose — the physical features themselves are — so Weight 3 is not reached.

Rule 6 is satisfied and Rule 5(b) is not. Several named sections contain a designated passage whose primary subject is the distribution of raw materials and water across geographies and which requires the student to register that distribution: 'The Urals' closes on a passage listing iron ore, copper, zinc, platinum, gold, coal, oil and natural gas; 'The Colorado Plateau' names coal, oil, natural gas, uranium and copper as the basis of the region's economic importance; the Alps passage names iron, copper, lead, rock salt, graphite, gypsum and magnesite; the Andes passage names copper, zinc, silver and lithium; and the Tibetan Plateau is identified as holding the largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions. These are designated passages within landform sections rather than a dedicated section or architecturally distinct activity block, and the chapter enumerates resource endowments as a closing beat for each landform without comparing distribution across geographies or requiring the student to operate on the pattern — so the development is present but not substantive in the Rule 5(b) sense.
